uncited: Tree-based structures represent volumetric data by recursively subdividing the spatial domain into hierarchical nodes, storing data only in occupied regions to achieve compression proportional to sparsity .
They solve the storage and traversal inefficiency of dense 3D grids by allowing ray marching to skip empty space efficiently .

This family sets itself apart from siblings like [Hash Grids](936-hash-grids.md) by maintaining explicit spatial hierarchy and from [Brick-based Hierarchical Storage](2793-brick-based-hierarchical-storage.md) by typically operating at the voxel level rather than fixed-size blocks, though variants like [Compact pointer tree](844-compact-pointer-tree.md) introduce variable branching factors to optimize memory .
**Recursive Subdivision:** The 3D domain is recursively divided into sub-volumes.
In standard octrees, each node has 8 children.
**Sparsity Encoding:** Empty regions are represented by null pointers or absence of children, rather than storing zero-valued voxels.
**Hierarchical Traversal:** Rendering or access requires traversing from the root to the leaf.
**Spatial Locality:** Children of a node are spatially contiguous.
**Subtree Merging:** The core differentiator of the DAG family is the identification of structurally identical subtrees (isomorphic nodes) and their replacement with a single shared instance.
This transforms the tree topology into a graph where multiple parents may reference the same child node, eliminating redundancy .
Tree-based structures originated as a solution to the memory limitations of dense volumetric grids.
Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) became a standard representation for high-resolution volumetric data in the early 2000s, popularized by work on ray casting and isosurface extraction .
The concept of merging identical subtrees to form DAGs was introduced to further compress redundant geometric structures .
Compact pointer trees and other variants have been developed more recently to address the specific constraints of GPU memory and real-time rendering of massive datasets .
